teaching_notes: Beat 1 exists to put the whole claim on one screen before any of it is argued: the base column, one column earned by doubling, the arc that says × 2, and the two cross products landing on the same number. The class should be asked out loud what must happen to the bottom row when the top row jumps BEFORE the beat is advanced — that ask is yours to make, not the screen's, and the screen never asks it.

Beat 2 is the beat the misconception hides in. Four does not divide ten, so a class that believes a table only works when one column divides into the next expects this one to fail. It is accepted, its factor is printed as the exact fraction 5/2, and — the part that carries the argument — its column is outlined in exactly the same accent as beat 1's whole-number column. Same colour IS the argument; say it.

Beat 3 refutes the additive route inside the table rather than beside it. Both rows gained 4, so the DIFFERENCE was preserved and the ratio was not: the drift prints as 2 : 3 → 3 : 4 and the two cross products land on 32 and 36. Let the class read those two unequal numbers aloud before you name the rule. Do not state the rule while the drift is still animating.

media.title: Two Numbers, One Comparison
media.context: This hook opens the topic on ratios. Students know the shared factor. The film must not define a ratio and must not explain equivalent ratios.
media.description: A lemonade jug is mixed as two cups of syrup for every five cups of water. Written as two to five it is one drink, and flipped to five to two it is a completely different one.
media.teaching_notes: Learning objective: Read and write a ratio, and understand why the order of its terms matters. Key teaching points: 1) A ratio compares two quantities by division. 2) The order of the terms says which quantity comes first. 3) Reversing the terms describes a different situation. 4) Multiplying both terms by the same number gives an equivalent ratio. Common misconceptions: 1) Students often treat a ratio as an unordered pair. 2) Students often read a ratio as a difference between the quantities. Pause points: 0:25, at the end of now flip it: ask which of the two drinks the class would rather have. 0:25, just before the open question: ask what the two numbers are actually counting. Questions to ask: before viewing, ask what two to five means here. After viewing, ask what would happen with four cups of syrup.

      at 2.1 s  Create(s1_axis) over 0.8 s, to lay the common baseline.
      at 3.9 s  GrowFromEdge(s1_bars) over 1.6 s, lag_ratio 0.25, to grow every bar up from the baseline.
      at 6.5 s  Write(s1_bars) over 1.0 s, lag_ratio 0.2, to put the value and the name on each bar.
      at 8.6 s  FadeIn(s1_barnote) over 0.8 s, to state the observation the scene has just made.
      at 10.4 s  FadeOut(s1_axis, s1_bars, s1_barnote) over 0.6 s, lag_ratio 0.05, to clear the frame, keeping only what carries on.
      Narration: "A lemonade jug is mixed as two cups of syrup for every five cups of water, and that gets written down as two to five."
      Persists into the next scene: s1_caption.

    Scene 2. Now flip it
      Duration: 13 seconds.
      On screen at the start: s1_caption.
      Beats:
      at 0.2 s  ReplacementTransform(s1_caption, s2_caption) over 0.9 s, to carry the caption forward rather than redrawing it.
      at 2.3 s  Create(s2_axis) over 0.8 s, to lay the common baseline.
      at 4.3 s  GrowFromEdge(s2_bars) over 1.6 s, lag_ratio 0.25, to grow every bar up from the baseline.
      at 7.0 s  Write(s2_bars) over 1.0 s, lag_ratio 0.2, to put the value and the name on each bar.
      at 9.2 s  FadeIn(s2_barnote) over 0.8 s, to state the observation the scene has just made.
      at 11.2 s  FadeOut(s2_axis, s2_bars, s2_barnote) over 0.6 s, lag_ratio 0.05, to clear the frame, keeping only what carries on.
      Narration: "Flip the two numbers over to five to two and the drink changes completely, from something refreshing into something that nobody in the room could possibly finish."
      Persists into the next scene: s2_caption.

    Scene 3. The open question
      Duration: 10 seconds.
      On screen at the start: s2_caption.
      Beats:
      at 0.2 s  AddTextLetterByLetter(s3_question) over 1.8 s, to let the question land word by word.
      at 3.3 s  Create(s3_rule) over 0.6 s, to underline the question.
      at 5.2 s  FadeIn(s3_qsub) over 0.7 s, to name where the student will go looking.
      at 7.3 s  Circumscribe(s3_question) over 1.4 s, to hold the question as the closing image.
      Narration: "So why should the order of the two numbers change the whole meaning of the comparison? Try the Ratio Strip and see."
      Persists into the next scene: nothing, this is the last scene.

  ANIMATION RULES
    Prefer animation over narration wherever a concept can be shown.
    Every scene contains at least one transformation that carries meaning.
    No scene holds a static frame for more than 3 seconds.
    Reveal progressively; never dump a finished diagram in one Create.
    On-screen text minimal; no paragraph of prose on screen at any time.
    Objects that persist across scenes are transformed, never recreated.
    No decorative-only animation.

  MATHEMATICAL ACCURACY, highest priority
    100 percent accurate to NCERT Ganita Prakash for Class 8. Correct
    notation, terminology, symbols and labels as used in the Class 8
    textbook. Proportions true wherever proportion carries meaning; if a
    figure is not to scale it must say so on screen. No transformation may
    pass through a mathematically false intermediate state.

  LANGUAGE
    British spelling. No em dash and no en dash anywhere, in narration or on
    screen. Readable aloud by a student of this grade. Indian names and places
    for any person or setting.

  NEGATIVE CONSTRAINTS
    No value, label or claim absent from the truth model.
    No revealing of the rule, formula or answer anywhere in this hook.
    No worked solution, no general statement of the method.
    No text outside the safe margin, no overlapping labels.
    No external assets, watermarks or branding.
    No particles, sparkles or glow.

  SELF-CHECK BEFORE OUTPUT
    1. Scene durations sum to exactly 35 seconds across 3 scenes.
    2. Every number, count and label on screen appears in the truth model and nowhere else.
    3. Every mobject named in a beat is declared in the inventory before it is used.
    4. Every persisting mobject is transformed into its next form, never recreated.
    5. No scene holds a static frame for more than 3 seconds.
    6. All geometry lies within x in [-6.8, 6.8] and y in [-3.8, 3.8]; nothing is cropped.
    7. No label overlaps another label; buff at least 0.2 everywhere.
    8. British spelling throughout, and no em dash or en dash in narration or on screen.
    9. The final frame is the open question, with no rule, method or answer shown.
    10. The named tool is handed to the student in the closing narration.

topics.summary: A ratio a : b compares two quantities, with a and b its terms and order carrying meaning. Multiplying or dividing both terms by the same number builds equivalent ratios that keep the same multiplicative relationship.

content.text: A ratio a : b compares two quantities. The numbers a and b are called the terms of the ratio. We read a : b as a units of the first quantity for every b units of the second quantity. Dividing the first term by the second tells how many times as much the first is: 8 : 2 means the first is 4 times the second. The order matters, because 8 : 2 and 2 : 8 compare the quantities the opposite way round.

content.text: Two ratios are equivalent when they describe the same relationship. To build a ratio equal to a given one, multiply both terms by the same number, or divide both terms by the same number. For example 4 : 5 times 3 is 12 : 15, and both say the same thing. To test whether two ratios are equal, find the factor that carries the first terms onto each other and check that the same factor carries the second terms too. Adding the same amount to both terms does not keep the ratio equal, because it changes how many times one term is of the other.

learning_objectives.objective_text: Students will be able to infer what a comparison written as a : b means through observation and reasoning, and determine that a and b are its terms, that it reads as a units of the first quantity for every b units of the second, and that dividing the first term by the second tells how many times as much the first is. They will explain that a : b and b : a describe different comparisons because the order of the terms carries the meaning.
Examine the worked examples of a ratio compares two quantities, across different cases.
Examine the practised examples and practice questions involving a ratio compares two quantities, across different cases.

Students will be able to infer what keeps two ratios describing the same relationship through observation and reasoning, and determine that multiplying or dividing both terms by the same number produces an equal ratio, while a single shared factor carries one ratio onto another. They will explain that a ratio names a multiplicative relationship preserved only when both terms are scaled by the same factor, so adding the same amount to each term breaks the equality.
Examine the worked examples of equivalent ratios by scaling, across different cases.

media.title: The simplest form of a ratio
media.context: A ratio is simplest when its terms are the smallest whole numbers keeping the same comparison, reached by dividing both by their highest common factor. The worked example reduces 48 : 36. The figure finds the HCF and divides.

content.text: A ratio is in its simplest form when its terms are the smallest whole numbers that keep the same comparison. To reach it, divide both terms by their highest common factor, the HCF, which is the largest number that divides both. For 48 : 36 the HCF is 12, so the simplest form is 4 : 3. You must divide both terms by the same number, and it is simplest only when no number bigger than one divides both terms.

content.text: Two ratios are proportional when they describe the same relationship. To test them, reduce each to its simplest form and check whether the two forms are the same. If they match, the ratios are proportional; if they differ, they are not. When 4 : 5 and 16 : 20 both reduce to 4 : 5 we write 4 : 5 :: 16 : 20, using the :: symbol to mean is proportional to. Adding or subtracting the same number from the terms does not keep ratios proportional, because that changes the multiplicative comparison.

learning_objectives.objective_text: Students will be able to infer what makes a ratio as simple as it can be through observation and reasoning, and determine that dividing both terms by their highest common factor reaches the simplest form, where no whole number larger than one divides both terms. They will explain that dividing both terms by the same number keeps the comparison equal, while dividing the terms by different numbers changes the comparison and destroys the ratio.

Students will be able to infer what makes two ratios proportional through observation and reasoning, and determine that reducing each to its simplest form and checking that the forms match confirms a proportion, written as a : b :: c : d. They will explain that proportional ratios share one multiplicative relationship, so identical simplest forms prove proportion while adding the same amount to the terms does not.

media.title: Double Number Line
media.context: CBSE Class 8, new NCERT Ganita Prakash Ch 7 'Proportional Reasoning-1', the section on finding the missing fourth term. The class has met equivalent ratios and can read a value off a number line. The chapter's own word is the FACTOR OF CHANGE, so the tool says 'multiplier (the factor of change)' on first use in a mode and then 'multiplier'. The words rate, unit rate, constant of proportionality, k and the symbol ∝ belong to Part-2 Ch 3 and appear nowhere in this tool; the tool says 'the cost of 1 kilogram'. Cross multiplication (a : b = c : d exactly when a × d = b × c) is the chapter's own verification and is the tool's grading rule. The double number line itself is an NCETM/CCSS representation rather than an NCERT figure, so the class is meeting the picture for the first time and it is drawn to the standard convention.

overview.concept: Two quantities that scale together can be drawn on parallel lines whose ticks are locked by the ratio. Moving to a new value on one line multiplies the other by the same factor, so the unknown is found by naming that multiplier rather than by adding along the line.

overview.uiOverview: Lines fill the main panel one above the other with the readouts beneath. On a 390 px frame the lines rescale rather than scrolling, so both markers stay visible. The Finish button renders ONLY in Practice and Free Play, gated positively on the mode. The HOST renders the mode selector, the language switcher and the mute in its own bar; this tool does not draw them and never lists the mode selector as a student control.
overview.neverRemove: Do not show the partner value while a prediction is still open, and never let the two lines move independently. Independent lines would make a wrong pairing drawable.
overview.predictFirst: Step 1 of every mode that teaches opens with the CONTENT HIDDEN. The student commits a prediction before the tool shows any result, marked answer, filled table or read out. Committing emits prediction_made, which unlocks step 1 so the real result animates in BESIDE the guess.
overview.flowOfUnderstanding: Predict, then observe, then compare, then conclude. The lines are locked to one scale factor, so a position means the same proportion on both. Multiplying the first quantity by k moves the position by k, which multiplies the second by k as well. That is why naming the multiplier is the whole method, and why a mismatched placement cannot be drawn at all. Concept reveals the idea in 3 beats, Learn works the five checkpoints solved, Practice serves six drawn questions scored, and Free Play unlocks everything with nothing required.

learnMode.checkpointPlan: ML1 (Easy, Edge Case): The pairing is built into the picture, which is why the thinking goes into the multiplier. Breaks: Treating the two lines as independent, so a value is read off one without its partner. ML2 (Medium, Conceptual): Steps along the lines are multiplications, so the same number cannot be added to both. Breaks: Building up by repeated addition without noticing the multiplier. ML3 (Medium, Edge Case): The unit value is reached by dividing, which is the same locking rule with a multiplier below 1. Breaks: Believing the unit value needs a rule of its own. ML4 (Hard, Edge Case): A base pair has to name a real amount on each line before it can lock anything. Breaks: Believing any pair of matching values can serve as a base pair. ML5 (Hard, Conceptual): The multiplier carries no unit, which is why one number moves both lines. Breaks: Believing kilograms and rupees need different multipliers because they measure different things.

conceptMode.summary: Concept, agent driven, 3 teaching beats. Beat 1 opens with 3 kilograms marked against 90 rupees and asks where 7 kilograms will fall. Beat 2 drags the marker to 7 and its partner lands at 210, with the multiplier printed between the two pairs. Beat 3 halves the known pair instead, showing that the same locking works downwards and for fractions. The agent advances with next() / prev() / gotoStep and can compose a beat with setBasePair, moveMarker, showMultiplier and say. No drag: the agent moves a marker by value.

conceptMode.teacherCallPlan: Call 1. Open on the two locked lines with the base pair marked and no target placed, and ask the class to say out loud where the larger quantity will fall on the lower line. Commit the class answer on the prediction pad. Target: the base pair only. Never move a marker before the prediction is committed. Call 2. Drag the marker to the target quantity and let its partner land, then point at the multiplier as it writes itself into the gap between the pairs. Targets: the target quantity and the multiplier readout. Read both numbers from the tool's own state and never from this plan. Call 3. Halve the base pair instead and point at the two markers arriving together, so the same lock is seen working for a factor below 1. Targets: the halved pair and the multiplier readout. Name the unit value only after the markers have settled.

hunts: UNIT TICK: find the pair where the first line reads 1 and say what multiplier took you there.
OFF THE RANGE: drag a marker past the end of the drawn line and say what the tool did to the scale.
FRACTION HUNT: find three targets whose multiplier is not a whole number and write each as a fraction.
BLOCKED BASE: find a base pair the tool refuses and say what it could not fix.

observationsAndConclusions.why: Steps along locked lines are multiplications, so the same number cannot simply be added to both
observationsAndConclusions.observe: Adding the same number to both quantities lands on a position the lines will not draw
observationsAndConclusions.conclusion: An additive step is not a small error in a proportional situation, it is the wrong kind of move

media.description: Two horizontal number lines are drawn one above the other on a plain ground, kilograms on the top line and rupees on the bottom, with 0 aligned at the left end of both and one arrowhead at the right end of each. Their ticks are locked into vertical columns by a single base pair, so one POSITION names one value on each line at once and a pair that is not in the ratio has nowhere to sit. A pinned dashed column marks the base pair and a solid accent column carries the current pair, with both values printed in the band between the lines. When the current pair is not the base pair the factor of change writes itself into two identical curved arrows — one above the top line and one below the bottom line — as '×' followed by a hand-typeset stacked fraction in lowest terms, which is what makes 'one number moves both lines' visible. A proposed pair that is NOT in the ratio is drawn as a ghost segment joining its own two dots, and that segment SLANTS off the locked vertical column: the additive step the student was tempted by fails on screen instead of being contradicted in a caption. A base pair containing zero is refused, with two different candidate scales drawn faintly on the lower line to show that 0 and 0 fixes nothing. In Free Play the student drags either marker, steps it past the drawn end so the lines rescale together, drops labelled ticks that keep a pair permanently on screen with both values printed, resets the base ratio, jumps to the 1 kg tick, and types the multiplier to have it graded separately from the partner value.

mods.learn: Learn, teacher operated. The worked items arrive in props.learnQuestions, mandatory checkpoints first. Each item sets the known pair and the target from its own numbers, shows the question, then reveals the partner value, the multiplier and the answer together as one beat. Prev / Next move between items.
mods.ai_demo: Concept, agent driven, 3 teaching beats. Beat 1 opens with 3 kilograms marked against 90 rupees and asks where 7 kilograms will fall. Beat 2 drags the marker to 7 and its partner lands at 210, with the multiplier printed between the two pairs. Beat 3 halves the known pair instead, showing that the same locking works downwards and for fractions. The agent advances with next() / prev() / gotoStep and can compose a beat with setBasePair, moveMarker, showMultiplier and say. No drag: the agent moves a marker by value.

Scored, with a star finish and a Review phase that walks every item showing the student's placement, the correct partner and the multiplier that settles it.

concept.notation: A double number line has one line per quantity with matched ticks. Two values at the same position are a pair in the ratio.
concept.statement: Two quantities that scale together can be drawn on parallel lines whose ticks are locked by the ratio. Moving to a new value on one line multiplies the other by the same factor, so the unknown is found by naming that multiplier rather than by adding along the line.
prerequisites: reading a value from a number line
misconceptions: Building up by repeated addition without noticing the multiplier.
Treating the two lines as independent, so a value is read off one without its partner.
concept.why_it_is_true: The lines are locked to one scale factor, so a position means the same proportion on both. Multiplying the first quantity by k moves the position by k, which multiplies the second by k as well. That is why naming the multiplier is the whole method, and why a mismatched placement cannot be drawn at all.
worked_numbers: 3 kilograms at 90 rupees: the multiplier to 7 kilograms is 7 over 3, so the cost is 210.
Halving the pair gives 1.5 kilograms at 45 rupees, using a multiplier of one half.
The unit value is 1 kilogram at 30 rupees, reached by dividing both by 3.

answer_key.worked: From 3 kilograms at 90 rupees, 7 kilograms costs 210, using the multiplier 7 over 3.
answer_key.practice: Computed per item at runtime from the drawn lines: the partner value as an exact fraction, the multiplier between the pairs, and the unit value.
answer_key.precision: The ratio is stored as a numerator and denominator pair. Pixel positions are derived and never stored, so resizing cannot introduce drift.
answer_key.ground_truth: partner(base, value) = value times the base ratio, as an exact fraction. multiplier(from, to) = the exact ratio between them. unitValue(base) = the second quantity per one of the first.

blackboard.rule: Any theorem, derivation, proof, formula or numerical calculation that takes MORE THAN TWO mathematical steps is written on the blackboard step by step, one step below the previous one, in logical order.

modes.ai: The agent narrates while the board fills; the board never runs ahead of the narration.
modes.learn: The board is the reveal. Before reveal() it is empty; on reveal it fills line by line, then the answer lands last.
modes.normal: No board unless the student asks the tool to settle something, then the same line by line fill.
modes.practice: The board stays empty until the answer is checked, then fills line by line as the explanation.

blackboard.for_a_proof: State the claim first, then write and explain each step in sequence, then close on the conclusion.
blackboard.readability: Keep the board clean and uncrowded, at Class 8 reading level, with the same symbols the scene uses.
blackboard.applies_when: The explanation runs to more than two mathematical steps. Two steps or fewer may be written together.
blackboard.for_a_calculation: Show the complete working line by line, including every intermediate value, before the final answer is shown.
blackboard.one_step_per_line: Never show all the steps at once and never combine two calculations into one line. One calculation per line.
blackboard.source_of_the_lines: The `steps` array of the Learn checkpoint or Practice question on screen IS the blackboard, in order. Render one array entry per line. It is gated at build time: no entry carries two calculations.
blackboard.builds_progressively: The board fills line by line as the explanation is given, so the student can see how each step follows from the one above it. A line already written stays on the board.

edge_cases.case: A target beyond the drawn range
edge_cases.tool_behaviour: The lines rescale together so the target fits, and the tool says the scale changed rather than silently redrawing.

edge_cases.case: An attempt to move one marker alone
edge_cases.tool_behaviour: Impossible by construction, because the lines are locked. The partner always moves, which is what makes a wrong placement undrawable.

edge_cases.tool_behaviour: Blocked with the reason on screen, since a zero cannot fix a scale between the two lines.

basePair.description: The known pair that fixes the scale between the two lines.

questions.description: Replaces the built in practice bank. Items are {kind:'find_partner', base:number[], target:number} | {kind:'name_multiplier', from:number, to:number} | {kind:'unit_value', base:number[]} | {kind:'choice', prompt, options[], correct, explain}.

showMultiplier.description: Print the multiplier between the known pair and the current position, which is the quantity the method rests on.

constraints: The two lines are always locked to the same scale factor, so a marker cannot be placed without its partner moving.
The ratio is stored as a numerator and denominator pair, and pixel positions are derived rather than stored, so resizing introduces no drift.
Partner values are exact fractions and are displayed as fractions rather than rounded decimals.
A base pair containing zero is blocked with the reason on screen, since it cannot fix a scale.
When a target lies outside the drawn range the lines rescale together and the tool says the scale changed.

extra.concept_only: Concept carries no questions of its own. Its beats reveal the idea and then run one reasoning beat each, and every number the agent says is read from state.truth.

ai.shows: Both lines with their locked ticks, both markers, the multiplier readout, the teacher caption, and discrete step navigation (Prev / Step k of 3 / Next) with a progress bar.
steps: Predict: 3 kilograms is marked against 90 rupees and the target is not placed. The class commits where 7 kilograms will fall, out loud, and the teacher commits it on the pad. prediction_made unlocks the beat.

Scale down: the known pair is halved, giving 1.5 and 45, so the same locking is seen working for a fraction.

play_modes: UNIT TICK: find the pair where the first line reads 1 and say what multiplier took you there.
OFF THE RANGE: drag a marker past the end of the drawn line and say what the tool did to the scale.
FRACTION HUNT: find three targets whose multiplier is not a whole number and write each as a fraction.
BLOCKED BASE: find a base pair the tool refuses and say what it could not fix.
normal.parameter_freedom: Every adjustable parameter is unlocked inside its invariant limits, nothing is scored, nothing progresses, and no question is posed. The student sets the values, and may pose their own question and let the tool settle it, because the tool keeps computing and showing its invariants the whole time. The hunts below are starting points, not a syllabus.

shared_state.note: Exactly what getState() returns and what rides every {type:'state'} emit. The teacher agent reads these field names, so they are a contract: renaming one silently breaks narration.

aiModeCalls.steps: next() / prev() / gotoStep(index) over the Concept beats; playDemo() auto runs them all
aiModeCalls.description: In Concept the agent orchestrates the demonstration from these calls. next() / prev() / gotoStep drive the 3 built in beats; the component calls let the agent branch a beat, for example moving to a value a child names and printing the multiplier it needed.

postmessage.note: The tool emits {type:'ready', toolId} on mount and commands sent before it are DROPPED. Every windowMethod is also reachable as a command method.

agent_control.operator_note: Concept (ai) and Learn are TEACHER operated. The agent calls the step verbs and narrates; the class watches and answers out loud. No beat in these two modes may carry operate-the-control copy (no 'tap your guess', 'press Check', 'drag the marker'). Keep the thinking half of the sentence ('Predict first', 'Say your answer out loud first') and drop the device half. Practice and Free Play are student operated and address the student directly.

predict_first.rule: Step 1 of every mode that teaches opens with the CONTENT HIDDEN. The student commits a prediction before the tool shows any result, marked answer, filled table or read out. Committing emits prediction_made, which unlocks step 1 so the real result animates in BESIDE the guess.
predict_first.scope: Step 1 only. Steps 2..N use the ordinary reveal gate: scene and question shown, answer hidden until reveal.
mechanism: a prediction state field on the shared state
a prediction_made event listed in events[]
the emit fires once per step 1, never re-asked on later steps

terminal_event.name: finished
terminal_event.note: The host treats name === 'completed' || name === 'finished' as end of activity and writes the lesson summary. Emit 'finished' exactly once, guarded by a one shot ref that only reset() re-arms; the celebration overlay and chime sit OUTSIDE the guard so a second tap re-opens them. Never emit a bare 'completed', and never name a progress event '*_completed'. Progress events are named for what happened (step_done, example_done, bank_done). The Finish button renders ONLY in practice and normal, gated on the MODE, never on operatorMode.
terminal_event.firedBy: the last item of the active bank being answered, or the student pressing Finish

steps: The lock is the number of rupees that goes with one kilogram.
That number comes from dividing the second value of the base pair by the first.
Dividing 0 by 0 names no number at all, so no scale is fixed.
Every pair of lines would then fit the base pair equally well.
So the tool blocks it and says a base pair needs a real amount on each line.

steps: A position on the lines means the same share of the way along on both.
Moving to a position that is 3 times as far along multiplies the first quantity by 3.
It multiplies the second by 3 as well, because it is the same position.
The units differ but the multiplier is a pure number and carries no unit.
That is why naming the multiplier is the whole of the method.
items.answer: Because a multiplier is a pure number, so it acts on the position and not on the units

teaching_notes: Beat 1 exists to make the LOCK visible before any arithmetic. Both markers sit on the base pair, one vertical connector joins them, and the class is asked out loud what would have to happen to the rupees if the kilograms moved. Nothing about a multiplier is said yet — the point of the beat is that a position, not a number, is the object being moved.

Beat 2 is the whole method in one motion. The pair travels to 7 kg and ₹210, and the SAME '× 7/3' writes itself above the top line and below the bottom line. Two identical arrows for two different units is the argument that the multiplier carries no unit; point at both before naming the answer.

Beat 3 carries the idea to its useful edge rather than repeating it: the pair is halved instead, so the multiplier is 1/2, the markers travel back towards zero, and the 1 kg tick is shown to be an ordinary tick at ₹30. The unit value is not a separate rule, and the class should hear that said while the marker is still moving.

media.title: Finding the Number That Fits
media.context: This hook opens the topic on finding a missing term. Students know equivalent ratios. The film must not give the missing amount and must not describe cross multiplication.
media.description: A recipe for four people must stretch to twelve, and one quantity has been left blank. The numbers march up by a shared factor and the missing amount snaps into place.
media.teaching_notes: Learning objective: Find a missing term in a proportion using the factor of change or cross multiplication. Key teaching points: 1) Two proportional pairs are linked by one factor. 2) That factor is found by dividing the two known matching values. 3) Multiplying the other known value by it gives the missing term. 4) Cross multiplication does the same work in one line. Common misconceptions: 1) Students often add the difference instead of multiplying by the factor. 2) Students often cross multiply the wrong pair of terms. Pause points: 0:23, at the end of a shared factor: ask what four has to be multiplied by to reach twelve. 0:23, just before the open question: ask what the missing quantity must be. Questions to ask: before viewing, ask how they would stretch a recipe from four to ten. After viewing, ask where the factor comes from.

media.title: Why Adding the Same Number to Both Terms Breaks Proportion

media.description: A 2D whiteboard walkthrough contrasting additive and multiplicative change on a ratio. Neelima aged 3 and her mother aged 30 appear first, with the ratio 3 : 30 reducing to 1 : 10. Nine years pass on an animated clock. Neelima is 12 and her mother 39; the ratio 12 : 39 reduces to 4 : 13. A red cross appears over the attempted equality 1 : 10 equals 4 : 13. The video then contrasts with multiplicative scaling: 3 : 30 times 2 gives 6 : 60, which reduces back to 1 : 10 with a green tick. A closing caption reads 'Same factor preserves ratio; same addition does not.'

Pause at 85 seconds and ask 'Now try multiplying both by 2 - what do you expect?' - this is the attempt-before-reveal moment contrasting the two operations. After the final scene, ask 'In one sentence, why did adding 9 years to both sides break the proportion, but multiplying both by 2 kept it?'

topics.summary: With three of four linked terms known, the missing fourth is found by the factor of change carrying the first term to the third, and confirmed by cross multiplication, where a : b :: c : d holds exactly when a times d equals b times c.

content.text: In a proportion a : b :: c : d, the same factor changes a into c and b into d. To find a missing fourth term, first find the factor of change by dividing the third term by the first, c divided by a. Then multiply the second term b by that same factor to get d. For 8 : 12 :: 24 : ?, the factor is 24 divided by 8 = 3, so the missing term is 12 times 3 = 36. The factor may grow the terms or shrink them.

content.text: When a : b :: c : d, the diagonal products are equal: a times d equals b times c. This is called cross multiplication. It works because c is a times the factor of change and d is b times the same factor, so both products equal a times b times that factor. Cross multiplication gives a quick way to check a proportion and to find a missing term: if a : b :: c : d then d equals b times c divided by a. Always pair opposite corners, not the two terms you can see side by side.

learning_objectives.objective_text: Students will be able to infer what connects the two known ratios of a proportion through observation and reasoning, and determine the missing fourth term of a : b :: c : ? by finding the factor that carries the first term to the third, then multiplying the second term by that same factor. They will explain that both terms of a proportion change by one shared factor, so the missing term follows at once when that factor is known.
Examine the worked examples of the missing term by the factor of change, across different cases.
Examine the practised examples and practice questions involving the missing term by the factor of change, across different cases.

Students will be able to infer what stays equal across a true proportion through observation and reasoning, and determine that a : b :: c : d holds exactly when a times d equals b times c, so a missing term follows by solving that equation. They will explain that the diagonal products match because both ratios share one factor of change, which makes cross multiplication a single reliable check for any proportion.

overview.goal: The student divides an amount in a stated ratio using equal parts and explains why the total number of parts matters.
overview.theme: Class 8 register: clean geometric line work, one accent plus one second accent, no decoration Setting: A single horizontal bar across the working ground, labelled with its total and waiting to be divided. Character: none, because this mount is an instrument. Premise: A class shares an amount in a two term ratio by cutting it into two pieces, and the bar is asked whether the pieces add back up.
overview.concept: To divide a total in a given ratio, first split it into as many equal parts as the ratio terms add to, then give each share its number of parts. The total number of parts is the sum of the terms, not the number of terms, which is why a two term ratio rarely means splitting into two.
overview.purpose: The student divides an amount in a stated ratio using equal parts and explains why the total number of parts matters.
overview.blackboard: Any theorem, derivation, proof, formula or numerical calculation that takes MORE THAN TWO mathematical steps is written on the blackboard step by step, one step below the previous one, in logical order. Never show all the steps at once and never combine two calculations into one line. One calculation per line.
overview.uiOverview: Bar across the main panel with the part value beneath and the share readouts under that. The wrong route bar appears below when shown. On a 390 px frame the bar keeps full width and the segments never fall below 12 px. The Finish button renders ONLY in Practice and Free Play, gated positively on the mode. The HOST renders the mode selector, the language switcher and the mute in its own bar; this tool does not draw them and never lists the mode selector as a student control.
overview.neverRemove: Do not compute any share while a prediction is still open, and never draw parts of unequal length in the correct route. Unequal parts would make the method meaningless.
overview.predictFirst: Step 1 of every mode that teaches opens with the CONTENT HIDDEN. The student commits a prediction before the tool shows any result, marked answer, filled table or read out. Committing emits prediction_made, which unlocks step 1 so the real result animates in BESIDE the guess.
overview.flowOfUnderstanding: Predict, then observe, then compare, then conclude. Every part must be the same size, or the shares would not be in the stated ratio. If one share is m parts and the other is n, then together they are m plus n parts, and those parts make up the whole. So the part value is the total divided by m plus n, and each share follows. Splitting into two parts named 2 and 3 makes parts of different sizes, which is why the shares then fail to add to the total. Concept reveals the idea in 3 beats, Learn works the five checkpoints solved, Practice serves six drawn questions scored, and Free Play unlocks everything with nothing required.

conceptMode.teacherCallPlan: Call 1. Open on the whole bar with its total labelled, the ratio stated and no parts drawn, and ask the class to say out loud how many equal parts are needed first. Commit the class number on the prediction pad. Target: the whole bar. Never split the bar before the prediction is committed. Call 2. Split the bar into the parts the ratio calls for and drag the group divider so the two groups match the two terms. Targets: the part count and the group divider. Read the part value and both shares from the tool's own readouts and never from this plan. Call 3. Turn on the wrong route so a second bar is split into as many pieces as there are terms, and point at the shortfall as the two shares are summed. Targets: the wrong route bar and the shortfall readout. Never say what the wrong route gets wrong before the sum has stopped short.

hunts: ADD THEM BACK: try the wrong route on three totals and record how far the shares land from the bar.
ZERO TERM: share an amount in a ratio with a zero in it and say why the bar still fills.
EXACT FRACTION: find a total the part count does not divide, and check the two shares still add up.
WORK BACKWARDS: hide the total, give a classmate one share and the ratio, and see if they can recover it.

observationsAndConclusions.why: Each share is a whole number of parts, so all the parts have to be the same size for the ratio to hold
observationsAndConclusions.observe: The bar is cut into as many equal parts as the terms add to, never into as many parts as there are terms
observationsAndConclusions.conclusion: The sum of the terms is a count of parts, which is why a two term ratio rarely means cutting in two

observationsAndConclusions.why: Unequal pieces named 2 and 3 do not carry the part value, so the shares no longer make up the whole
observationsAndConclusions.observe: The wrong route leaves the running total stopping short of the end of the bar
observationsAndConclusions.conclusion: Shares that fail to add back to the total prove the part count was wrong, without any need to be told

observationsAndConclusions.why: Rounding each share would change their sum, so the total would no longer be recovered
observationsAndConclusions.observe: A total the part count does not divide is kept as an exact fraction rather than rounded
observationsAndConclusions.conclusion: An awkward part value is not an impossible share; it is a share that must be kept exact

media.description: A single horizontal bar stands on the working ground with its total written above it and the ratio written at its far end. The bar is cut into equal segments generated from one division, so every part is identical to the pixel, and a heavier divider groups those parts into the shares the ratio names, each group tinted in its own accent with its value printed beneath it and its part count printed above. The value of one part sits under the middle of the bar, kept as a stacked fraction whenever the total does not divide evenly, and the add-back line closes the share-out the way an Indian classroom does. Turning on the wrong route draws a second bar beneath, cut into as many pieces as there are names in the ratio, with the run those pieces would actually demand drawn at the SAME unit from the SAME origin so it is seen bursting past the bar's own end, the overshoot printed in rupees. Three-term ratios run through the identical rule with the sum of all three terms as the part count, and a reverse problem leaves the total slot reading ? with the given share ringed across exactly its own segments, so the forward routine has nothing to divide and the part value has to be recovered first.

concept.notation: Sharing in the ratio m to n means m parts to one share and n to the other, out of m plus n equal parts in total.
concept.statement: To divide a total in a given ratio, first split it into as many equal parts as the ratio terms add to, then give each share its number of parts. The total number of parts is the sum of the terms, not the number of terms, which is why a two term ratio rarely means splitting into two.
prerequisites: reading a ratio as a comparison of parts
misconceptions: Dividing by the number of ratio terms rather than by the sum of the terms.
Sharing by the difference between the terms.
concept.why_it_is_true: Every part must be the same size, or the shares would not be in the stated ratio. If one share is m parts and the other is n, then together they are m plus n parts, and those parts make up the whole. So the part value is the total divided by m plus n, and each share follows. Splitting into two parts named 2 and 3 makes parts of different sizes, which is why the shares then fail to add to the total.
worked_numbers: 1200 in the ratio 2 to 3 needs 5 equal parts of 240, giving 480 and 720.
The wrong route splits into two parts and the shares do not add to 1200.
1200 in the ratio 1 to 2 to 3 needs 6 parts of 200, giving 200, 400 and 600.

answer_key.worked: 1200 shared in the ratio 2 to 3 needs 5 equal parts of 240, so the shares are 480 and 720.
answer_key.practice: Computed per item at runtime from the drawn bar: the part value and every share as an exact fraction, or the total when a share is given.
answer_key.precision: Exact rational arithmetic. When the total does not divide evenly the tool keeps fractions and says so rather than rounding silently.
answer_key.ground_truth: partValue(total, terms) = total divided by the sum of the terms, exactly. shares(total, terms) = each term times the part value. totalFromShare(share, term, terms) = share divided by term times the sum of the terms.

blackboard.rule: Any theorem, derivation, proof, formula or numerical calculation that takes MORE THAN TWO mathematical steps is written on the blackboard step by step, one step below the previous one, in logical order.

modes.ai: The agent narrates while the board fills; the board never runs ahead of the narration.
modes.learn: The board is the reveal. Before reveal() it is empty; on reveal it fills line by line, then the answer lands last.
modes.normal: No board unless the student asks the tool to settle something, then the same line by line fill.
modes.practice: The board stays empty until the answer is checked, then fills line by line as the explanation.

blackboard.for_a_proof: State the claim first, then write and explain each step in sequence, then close on the conclusion.
blackboard.readability: Keep the board clean and uncrowded, at Class 8 reading level, with the same symbols the scene uses.
blackboard.applies_when: The explanation runs to more than two mathematical steps. Two steps or fewer may be written together.
blackboard.for_a_calculation: Show the complete working line by line, including every intermediate value, before the final answer is shown.
blackboard.one_step_per_line: Never show all the steps at once and never combine two calculations into one line. One calculation per line.
blackboard.source_of_the_lines: The `steps` array of the Learn checkpoint or Practice question on screen IS the blackboard, in order. Render one array entry per line. It is gated at build time: no entry carries two calculations.
blackboard.builds_progressively: The board fills line by line as the explanation is given, so the student can see how each step follows from the one above it. A line already written stays on the board.

edge_cases.case: A total that does not divide evenly
edge_cases.tool_behaviour: Fractions are kept and the tool says the part value is not a whole number, rather than rounding and producing shares that do not add to the total.
Handled by the same rule, with the sum of all three terms as the part count, so the method is seen not to be a two term trick.
Available on purpose, and its shares visibly fail to add to the total. The failure is the argument and is never hidden.
One share is given and the total is unknown, which cannot be solved by the forward routine and forces reasoning back through the part value.
Allowed, giving that share nothing, and the tool states it rather than blocking, since it is a legitimate if unusual case.
